claims.text: Thermal activation drives Mg segregation into stable intermetallic compounds in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Mg-rich precipitates preferentially oxidize during high-temperature exposure.
Oxidation of Mg-rich precipitates produces a coherent MgO-rich passivation layer.
A coherent MgO-rich passivation layer improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates create local electrochemical inhomogeneities in aqueous environments.
Precipitate-induced electrochemical inhomogeneities can enhance localized corrosion relative to a homogeneous solid solution.
The initial alloy is a rapidly quenched metastable material with a predominantly homogeneous solid solution and minimal intermetallic segregation.
Controlled thermal aging or annealing induces Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation relative to the quenched state.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds nucleate during thermal exposure and constitute the structural mediator.
Thermodynamic driving forces in a multi-principal-element alloy promote local chemical segregation of Mg.
Mg-rich precipitates act as nucleation sites for a continuous MgO-rich surface layer.
Thermally aged alloys will have better high-temperature oxidation behavior than the as-quenched baseline.
Thermally aged alloys will exhibit altered, and potentially higher, localized aqueous-corrosion rates than the homogeneous baseline.
Processing parameters and service environments can alter phase evolution and the resulting oxidation and corrosion behavior.
The magnitude of oxidation and corrosion changes depends on intermetallic phase distribution and interfacial characteristics.
Temperature- and composition-dependent intermetallic phase formation and microstructural evolution have been observed in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
Processed Mg-Ti-Zn multi-principal-element alloys can contain intermetallic phases, including Mg21Zn25, or a predominantly Mg-rich phase.
Mg-Ti-Zn alloys exhibit measurable corrosion behavior in NaCl solution, and TiO2-rich surface-film formation can improve passivation.
